title: Bài sưu tầm 115 - Passage 1: The Hydraulic Architecture of Petra
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 115

The Hydraulic Architecture of Petra

Paragraph 1. Concealed deep within the dramatic rose-tinted sandstone canyons of southern Jordan, the ancient city of Petra was one of the most prosperous trading hubs of classical antiquity. Serving as the imperial capital of the Nabataean kingdom from the fourth century BCE to the early second century CE, Petra commanded the vital desert crossroads where the frankincense, myrrh, and silk caravan routes linking southern Arabia, Egypt, the Levant, and India intersected. However, Petra’s spectacular rock-cut monuments, including the iconic Treasury (Al-Khazneh), obscure an even greater technological triumph: the construction of a revolutionary hydraulic infrastructure that allowed twenty thousand inhabitants to thrive in a harsh desert basin receiving barely 150 millimetres of rainfall each year.

Paragraph 2. The geographic positioning of Petra presented the Nabataeans with a formidable hydrologic paradox. The city sits inside an arid sandstone bowl enclosed by jagged mountains, where seasonal water scarcity was an existential threat. Yet during the winter months, sudden, intense torrential downpours in the surrounding highlands produced catastrophic flash floods. Water collected rapidly on impermeable mountain plateaus and funneled violently into the Siq—the narrow, mile-long geological gorge that formed the sole ceremonial entrance into the city. Uncontrolled, these torrents drowned travelers, demolished masonry, and rendered the canyon unusable.

Paragraph 3. To mitigate this environmental hazard, Nabataean engineers executed an ambitious flood-prevention masterplan. At the northern portal of the Siq, they constructed an immense stone diversion dam, measuring over thirteen metres high, which blocked incoming floodwaters. Adjoining the dam, workers excavated an eighty-eight-metre-long bypass tunnel directly through the solid sandstone bedrock of Mount Khubtha, rerouting surging flash floods into a neighboring wadi and safely away from the city center.

Paragraph 4. Having eliminated the flood threat, the Nabataeans transformed the seasonal deluge into a permanent freshwater supply. Using chisels and natural gradient slopes, engineers carved an extensive network of open rock-cut channels and covered terra-cotta pipelines stretching across mountains for tens of kilometres. Water captured from distant natural springs, such as the legendary Ain Musa, was conducted into the urban core entirely through gravity. Ceramic piping sections were fitted together using watertight natural slaked-lime mortar and laid at an optimal descent gradient of four degrees. This specific engineering calculation maintained a stable, non-turbulent laminar flow, preventing water hammer damage and minimizing structural erosion of the conduits.

Paragraph 5. To guarantee year-round domestic and civic security, Nabataean engineers constructed hundreds of subterranean cisterns, reservoirs, and public basins across the city, capable of storing over forty million litres of water. Sedimentation tanks were strategically positioned along the conduit trajectories; as incoming water slowed inside these chambers, suspended sand and mineral debris settled to the floor, allowing only purified, crystal-clear water to flow forward. Consequently, Petra did not merely maintain basic hydration: the desert metropolis featured lavish public fountains, functioning thermal bathhouses, and lush, artificially irrigated tiered gardens with palm groves and ornamental reflection pools.

Paragraph 6. The decline of Petra’s hydraulic empire was ultimately brought about by changing trade dynamics and tectonic upheaval. Following the annexation of the Nabataean kingdom by Roman Emperor Trajan in 106 CE, imperial trade routes gradually shifted northward toward Palmyra and maritime transport along the Red Sea, eroding Petra’s commercial wealth. The fatal blow came in 363 CE, when a catastrophic earthquake leveled large sections of the city and shattered its subterranean aqueducts, cisterns, and water conduits. Unable to mobilize the labor and capital required to rebuild the intricate hydraulic infrastructure, the surviving population gradually dispersed, and Petra's stone wonders were slowly buried beneath desert sands.

groups.title: Questions 8–13
groups.instructions:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 115?
In boxes 8–13 on your answer sheet, write:
TRUE – if the statement agrees with the information
FALSE – if the statement contradicts the information
NOT GIVEN – if there is no information on this

steps: Đoạn 3: "...excavated an eighty-eight-metre-long bypass tunnel directly through the solid sandstone bedrock..."
Đoạn 4: "...was conducted into the urban core entirely through gravity."
Đoạn 4: "...laid at an optimal descent gradient of four degrees."
Đoạn 5: "Sedimentation tanks were strategically positioned along the conduit trajectories..."
Đoạn 5: "...fountains, functioning thermal bathhouses, and lush, artificially irrigated tiered gardens..."
Đoạn 6: "...when a catastrophic earthquake leveled large sections of the city and shattered its subterranean aqueducts..."

q8.text: Petra became wealthy by controlling the maritime trade routes along the Mediterranean coast.

steps: Đoạn 1: Petra làm giàu nhờ các tuyến đường bộ của đoàn lữ hành sa mạc (vital desert crossroads... caravan routes), không phải các tuyến hàng hải duyên hải Địa Trung Hải.

q9.text: The annual rainfall in the region of Petra was sufficient to sustain agriculture without irrigation.

steps: Đoạn 1 & 2: Lượng mưa chỉ 150mm/năm, khan hiếm nước là mối đe dọa sinh tồn (existential threat), không thể duy trì nông nghiệp nếu thiếu tưới tiêu.

q10.text: Nabataean builders used a specialized mortar to connect sections of clay pipes.

steps: Đoạn 4: "Ceramic piping sections were fitted together using watertight natural slaked-lime mortar..."

q11.text: The underground reservoirs in Petra were financed directly by Emperor Trajan.

steps: Đoạn 5 & 6: Nhắc đến việc Nabataean xây dựng các bể chứa và Trajan sáp nhập vùng đất vào năm 106 CE, nhưng không hề đề cập Trajan có chi tiền tài trợ các bể ngầm này hay không.

q12.text: The diversion dam near the entrance to the Siq was reconstructed during the twentieth century.

steps: Đoạn 3: Có nhắc đến con đập đá cao 13m của người Nabataean, nhưng không có thông tin về việc nó có được trùng tu ở thế kỷ 20 hay không.

q13.text: The economic prosperity of Petra began to decline before the earthquake of 363 CE.

steps: Đoạn 6: "...Following the annexation... in 106 CE, imperial trade routes gradually shifted... eroding Petra’s commercial wealth. The fatal blow came in 363 CE, when a catastrophic earthquake..." → Kinh tế đã suy thoái từ trước trận động đất năm 363 CE.
